snippet.title: The Weimar Hyperinflation — 4.2 Trillion Marks Per Dollar (1923)
snippet.description:
In November 1923, one US dollar bought 4.2 trillion German marks.

This is the story of how Germany's currency collapsed in a single year. The Treaty of Versailles imposed 132 billion gold marks in reparations on a country that had just lost a war. Then France occupied the Ruhr Valley — Germany's industrial heartland. The German government told workers to strike and kept paying their salaries. With printed money.

By October 1923, inflation was running at 29,500 percent per month. Wheelbarrows of cash to buy bread. Women burned currency for heat because it was cheaper than firewood. Those on fixed incomes were wiped out in months.

The crisis ended with the Rentenmark in November 1923. But an entire generation of German middle-class wealth had been erased. Scholars argue this trauma shaped the political conditions that made extremism possible a decade later.

This is the story of the worst currency collapse in all of recorded human history — and it wasn't Germany.
Most people think of Weimar Germany when they hear "hyperinflation." But Hungary's collapse in 1945–1946 made Germany look like a rounding error. At its peak, Hungary's monthly inflation rate hit 41 quadrillion percent. The government eventually printed a banknote worth 100 quintillion pengős — it was worth 20 cents on the day it was printed and nothing three weeks later.
But here's what nobody talks about: this wasn't purely an accident. Behind the collapse was a chain of decisions stretching from Versailles in 1920 to Budapest in 1946 — involving World War Two, a stolen gold reserve, a Soviet occupation, and a government that may have had reasons not to stop the printing press.

Die Hyperinflation 1923 in der Weimarer Republik ist ein historisches Beispiel für eine extreme Geldentwertung, bei der das Vertrauen in die Währung praktisch völlig verloren ging.

Die Reichsmark verlor rapide an Wert, da die Preise stiegen und Deutschland den Ersten Weltkrieg durch Kredite und Gelddrucken finanzierte. Der Vertrauensverlust in die Währung führte zu einer weiteren Preissteigerung.

Extreme Ausmaße der Inflation
 • 1914: 1 US-Dollar = 4,2 Mark.
 • 1923 (Nov.): 1 US-Dollar = 4,2 Billionen Mark!

Menschen schleppten Geld in Schubkarren oder nutzten Banknoten als Tapeten oder Brennmaterial.

snippet.title: 1923: Hyperinflation | GCSE History | Weimar Germany
snippet.description:
It’s 1923 and a goods shortage means that prices are rising like crazy.

#GCSEHistory​ #GCSERevision​ #WeimarGermany​

PATREON: https://www.patreon.com/alonglongtimeago

***---Useful resources---***

Revision Notes:
Inflation and hyperinflation
- goods shortages in early 1923 meant that prices went up - this is called inflation
- people had to pay more money to get what they needed
- government decisions made things worse
- the gov needed money to pay their debts but unemployment and failing factories meant they were getting less tax money
- 1919-23 gov income was a quarter of what was needed
- the gov resorted to printing more money
- 1923 gove had 300 paper mills and 2000 printing shops dedicated to printing more bank notes
- initially it made it easier to pay reparations
- but it made inflation worse
- vicious circle: prices rose more, more money printed, caused prices to rise again
- by 1923 prices where huge
- this extreme inflation is called hyperinflation
- price of a loaf of bread: 1919 1 mark, 1922, 100 marks, 1923 200 000 billion marks

the effects of hyperinflation

1) Normal Living became impossible
- printing presses couldn’t produce enough money
- people had to pin money to letters because stamps were useless
- they had to carry bundles of money in baskets and even wheelbarrows
- many workers were paid twice a day so they could rush out and buy goods before prices rose even more
- some shops refused to take money at all, asking for payment in kind (swapping goods)
- some people raided shops because they couldn’t afford food

2) Everyone suffered from shortages
- german marks became worthless for importing goods
- 1918 buying £1 worth of foreign goods cost 20 marks, by nov 1923, £1 worth of foreign goods cost 20 billion marks
- foreign suppliers refused to accept german marks for goods so imports dried up and shortages of food and other goods got worse for everyone

3) People with savings were hit hardest
- those with money in bank accounts, insurance policies or pensions had their saved money become worthless
- thus the middle classes were the worst affected

There were people who benefited from inflation
- people who had loans or took them out found that the value of the money they owed went down, e.g. some big businessmen borrowed money and profited because the value of their debts went down
- other people hoarded goods and then sold them for a large profit as prices went up
- foreign visitors also benefited, as the value of their own currency rose against the german mark, so they could buy much more with their money
- german people bitterly resented people who made money out of their suffering

the damage done
- after august 1923 a new chancellor gustav stresemann found solutions to some of the problems of 1923
- by this point however the political and economic turmoil from 1918 to 1923 had done its damage
- the WR was shown to be weak, it had been rescued by the freikorps in 1919 and workers striked in 1920, government forces had killed thousands of germans in order to stay in power
- all germans had suffered. most blamed the WR for their suffering, the middle classes which would normally be the bedrock of the republic suffered most
- extremist parties with private armies hostile to the republic had gained in strength

snippet.description:
In November 1923, one US dollar was worth about 4.21 trillion German marks. A loaf of bread that cost roughly 160 marks at the end of 1922 cost around 200 billion marks a year later. People burned banknotes for heat because the paper was cheaper than the firewood it could buy. This is not a story about a freak event. It is a story about a chain of decisions, each one defensible on its own, that ended with a nation's money turning into wallpaper. And the core mechanism behind it is exactly what every modern central bank is now built to prevent.

snippet.title: How Rational Decisions Destroyed Germany’s Economy | Weimar Germany Hyperinflation Explained
snippet.description:
When people talk about Weimar Germany, they usually talk about money.
Hyperinflation.
Worthless banknotes.
Numbers that stopped making sense.
But that is not what destroyed the country.
What collapsed first were people.
This video is not about charts or abstract economics.
It is about ordinary men and women who followed the rules, worked hard, saved their money — and still lost everything.
After World War I, Germany faced an impossible system:
war reparations paid in gold, a shattered economy, political instability, and decisions that made sense at the time.
No single choice was insane.
No single leader planned disaster.
Yet those rational decisions compounded into one of the most devastating economic collapses in modern history.

By 1923, money was everywhere — and food was not.
Savings evaporated.
The middle class disappeared.
Trust in institutions broke long before democracy did.
This is the human story behind Weimar Germany’s hyperinflation —
how economic collapse reshaped society, psychology, and the future of an entire nation.

Because when money fails, it doesn’t stop at the economy.

24. Oktober 1929: An der Wallstreet stürzen die Aktienkurse ins Bodenlose. Der Crash erfasst nahezu die ganze Welt – und bringt Armut, Arbeitslosigkeit und Chaos. 

Auch in der noch jungen Weimarer Republik liegt die Wirtschaft am Boden. Die Arbeitslosenquote steigt auf 30 Prozent. Erinnerungen an die Hyper-Inflation von 1923 werden wach, als ein Brot mehr als 200 Millionen Mark kostete. Menschen verkaufen ihr Hab und Gut für Spottpreise, um ihr Leben zu retten.  

Doch wie konnte es dazu kommen? Der Börsencrash ist das Ergebnis einer fatalen Kettenreaktion. Politische Entscheidungen bauten ein gefährliches Kartenhaus an den Börsen – unter anderem beeinflusst von der Euphorie der „Goldenen Zwanziger“. In den USA drängen viele Unternehmen an die Börse. Der Handel mit Aktien boomt. Doch die Aktienkäufe werden vielfach durch Kredite finanziert, die wiederum mit Aktien abgesichert werden. Es entsteht eine riesige Spekulationsblase, in deren Strudel auch schnell die Weimarer Republik gerät. Ein tragischer Dominoeffekt nimmt seinen Lauf.  

Unsere Doku rekonstruiert die Ursachen des beispiellosen Crashs, seine dramatischen Folgen für Wirtschaft und Bevölkerung – und klärt, warum die „Goldenen Zwanziger” für die meisten Menschen wenig mit der Realität zu tun hatten.

snippet.title: Hyperinflation 1923: Wie Deutschland im Geld ertrank & Weimar zerbrach | Analyse
snippet.description:
Im Jahr 1923 erlebte Deutschland eine Katastrophe, die bis heute als Mahnmal wirtschaftlicher Zerstörung dient: die Hyperinflation. Wie konnte es geschehen, dass alltägliche Güter Millionen, Milliarden oder gar Billionen Reichsmark kosteten? Dieses Video taucht tief in die Mechanismen und die verheerenden Folgen dieser beispiellosen Geldentwertung ein, die nicht nur die Ersparnisse einer ganzen Nation vernichtete, sondern auch das Fundament der jungen Weimarer Republik erschütterte.

Nach dem Ersten Weltkrieg und den harten Bedingungen des Versailler Vertrags sah sich Deutschland mit immensen Reparationsforderungen konfrontiert. Die Druckpressen liefen heiß, um die Staatsausgaben zu decken, doch die scheinbare Lösung wurde zum Verhängnis. Die Besetzung des Ruhrgebiets durch französische und belgische Truppen als Reaktion auf ausgebliebene Reparationszahlungen verschärfte die Krise dramatisch. Die Regierung rief zum passiven Widerstand auf und finanzierte die Löhne der streikenden Arbeiter, was die Inflation zusätzlich anheizte und das Vertrauen in die Währung endgültig zerstörte.

Historiker und Ökonomen debattieren bis heute intensiv über die wahren Ursachen und die Rolle der Akteure. Einige sehen die Hauptschuld bei den alliierten Siegermächten und ihren Reparationsforderungen, die eine untragbare Last für die deutsche Wirtschaft darstellten. Eine andere Perspektive betont die verfehlte Finanzpolitik der Reichsregierung, die durch exzessives Gelddrucken eine bewusste Strategie der Schuldenentwertung verfolgt haben soll, um die Reparationen obsolet zu machen. Wieder andere heben hervor, wie die psychologische Dynamik des Vertrauensverlusts und die Erwartungshaltung der Bevölkerung die Preisspirale unaufhaltsam beschleunigten, bis das Geld am Ende eines Tages nur noch bedrucktes Papier war. War es eine Verschwörung, ein politischer Schachzug oder eine Verkettung unglücklicher Umstände?

Diese umfassende Analyse beleuchtet die komplexen Zusammenhänge und die tiefgreifenden sozialen, wirtschaftlichen und politischen Konsequenzen der Hyperinflation, die das Fundament für spätere politische Extreme legte und das kollektive Gedächtnis Deutschlands nachhaltig prägte.

snippet.title: Weimar Berlin (1923): A Day During Hyperinflation
snippet.description:
What does hyperinflation actually feel like when you are living inside it?
This documentary follows a day in Weimar Berlin in 1923, when wages lost value by the hour and ordinary life had to move faster than money could collapse.

Weimar Berlin (1923): A Day During Hyperinflation is not just a story about giant numbers and economic charts. It is about the daily mechanics of monetary collapse: factory workers rushing to spend their pay, families waiting at factory gates for wages, pensioners watching savings disappear, and restaurants changing prices before a meal was even finished.

The video traces how Germany reached this point through war debt, reparations, the Ruhr occupation, passive resistance, and the political decision to keep paying striking workers by printing money. It then brings the crisis back down to street level in Berlin, where trams still ran, offices still opened, and the city still functioned — but every ordinary transaction had become surreal.

Along the way, this documentary explores the deeper social texture of the Weimar hyperinflation: barter replacing cash, foreign currency becoming a lifeline, black market exchange on Berlin streets, and the very unequal outcomes between workers, pensioners, asset holders, and industrial profiteers. It also shows how the Rentenmark stabilized prices quickly, while leaving behind a much deeper wound in trust, savings, and political culture.

If you’re interested in Weimar Germany, German hyperinflation, Berlin in 1923, the collapse of the Papiermark, or what daily life during hyperinflation really looked like, this video is built around that exact question. The focus is not just on how prices rose, but on how inflation destroyed predictability itself.

Some specific anecdotes, figures, and lived experiences vary depending on the source, especially by class, region, and access to foreign currency, but the broader pattern is well documented across contemporary accounts.

snippet.title: The Death of Money: Hyperinflation in Weimar Germany
snippet.description:
Book: When Money DIes by Adam Fergusson






The Anatomy of Monetary Collapse: Hyperinflation in the Weimar Republic and Successor StatesExecutive SummaryThe collapse of the German mark and the Austrian krone following the First World War serves as a definitive case study in the catastrophic consequences of deficit spending, the suspension of monetary discipline, and the prioritisation of "the soft option" by governing authorities. This analysis, synthesized from the historical records of the period, outlines a trajectory from gradual depreciation to a "delirium of milliards" where money ceased to function as a store of value or a medium of exchange.Critical Takeaways:

     
       •  The Illusion of Stability: Inflation was often misperceived by the public as a rise in the price of goods rather than a fall in the value of money. This led to a "flight from the currency" where the velocity of circulation increased, further accelerating the collapse.
       •  The Destruction of the Middle Class: While the working class could occasionally leverage unions for wage adjustments, the bourgeoisie and those on fixed incomes (pensioners, civil servants, academics) were systematically liquidated. Their life savings, invested in once-secure government bonds, became worthless.
       •  Political Radicalization: Monetary collapse acted as a "powerful engine of upheaval," fostering the conditions necessary for the rise of extremism. The erosion of social status and economic security fueled xenophobia, anti-Semitism, and a longing for "Spartan" authoritarian leadership.
       •  Institutional Failure: The Reichsbank, under the "mad" leadership of Rudolf Havenstein, operated under the fallacy that the flood of paper was a result—rather than a cause—of depreciation. This led to a cycle where the government printed money to meet its own deficits and the credit demands of industry, ultimately destroying the nation's moral and economic fabric.

snippet.title: How Inflation Quietly Becomes Hyperinflation
snippet.description:
Your parents could fill a whole grocery bag with a single twenty-dollar bill. The same bill barely covers lunch today — and the number on it never changed. That slow loss of value is **inflation**, and almost nobody can explain why it actually happens.

The honest answer isn't "prices go up." It's that money itself loses value — too much money chasing the same goods, every unit quietly diluted. This video builds inflation from first principles: the **two engines** (demand-pull and cost-push), the **wage-price spiral**, where new money actually comes from (it's typed into existence, not printed), the hidden tax that moves wealth from savers to borrowers — and the knife-edge where ordinary inflation tips into **hyperinflation**.

You'll see the US dollar lose **96%** of its value since 1913, Weimar Germany's wheelbarrows of cash in 1923, Zimbabwe's **$100,000,000,000,000** note that couldn't buy a week of groceries, why central banks deliberately aim for **~2%** instead of zero, and why cash under the mattress has lost more than half its buying power since 1990.

If you've ever wondered why your money buys a little less every year — and what would make it suddenly buy almost nothing — start here.

snippet.title: The Death of Money: The Weimar Hyperinflation Story
snippet.description:
In 1923, Germany experienced one of the most extreme economic collapses in modern history.

What began as war debt and political miscalculation turned into a hyperinflationary spiral that destroyed the value of the German Mark… and reshaped an entire society.

A loaf of bread cost billions. Savings disappeared overnight. Money became worthless paper—while trust, stability, and social order collapsed alongside it.

This is the story of the Weimar Hyperinflation:
how a modern, industrial nation lost control of its currency… and nearly lost control of reality itself.

From the Treaty of Versailles to the printing presses running 24/7, from desperate barter economies to the rise of political extremism—this is not just economic history.

It is a warning.
Because money is not just paper.
It is trust.
And when trust breaks… everything follows.

📉 Watch until the end to understand how the crisis was stopped—and why its “ghost” still shapes the world today.
